title: Homer, Teacher of Us All
author: Arts of Liberty
summary: A teacher writing for Arts of Liberty reflects on beginning Homer with his underclassmen and argues that Homer is the right first great author for postmodern students. Using C.S. Lewis's distinction between primary and secondary epic, he contrasts Virgil, whose pattern of history is political and almost propagandistic, with Homer, who is free of political and philosophical partisanship. Homer, he says, does not claim that history has an intelligible pattern, which partly aligns him with postmoderns who live with competing narratives and doubt. Drawing on Charles Taylor, Hannah Arendt, Christopher Dawson and T.S. Eliot, he suggests that the Christian view locates history's meaning in inward spiritual change rather than the outer political world. Homer's refusal to answer the questions of life and death, and his willingness to show people wrestling with them, makes him an indispensable first teacher toward the Delphic command to know thyself.
points: Following Lewis, primary epic like Homer's differs from secondary epic like Virgil's, which makes the pattern of history itself its political subject.
Reading every text through a political decryption key, usually a revolutionary one, spoils the reading experience and misses what the poem actually shows.
Homer accepts war and peace, love and hatred, life and death without excluding anything for the sake of an idea or allegiance, which is why later Western thinkers draw on him.
Students raised amid competing faiths and national myths share the postmodern predicament, and Homer meets them without forcing a pattern of history on them.
Homer shows people wrestling with mortality rather than answering for them, making him a fitting first author for students beginning to know themselves.
quotes: Homer, it seems to me, isn’t at all convinced that history has an intelligible pattern. I don’t mean that he actively disbelieves in such a pattern, which would align him with the postmoderns; I simply don’t think the question would ever have occurred to him.

Virgil’s pattern is political and his use of the past rhetorical, almost propagandistic. He’s a marvelous poet, but his poem is suffused throughout with a layer of political significance lacking in Homer.
That’s how some critics nowadays read everything, and it spoils the reading experience — especially because the political key is always presumed to be revolutionary.
Homer immortalized this full, contradictory vision of life as a common treasury from which all later Western thinkers have plundered only some things as worth keeping.
Whether we like it or not, even whether we admit it or not, we all suffer from the postmodern problem.

The political myths of other epics universalize given answers to the problem of life and death, but Homer refuses to answer: he’s content simply to show us men wrestling with the question — and therefore to show us ourselves.
Homer, therefore, is an indispensable first teacher for postmodern students seeking to fulfill the Delphic command to “know thyself.
